entries.title: Shoddy Polling in Battleground States Could Fuel Outsider 2028 Candidates
entries.summary: The political class has leaned heavily on polling data to help them make decisions — now they’re wondering about its relevance.
entries.content:
As the Democratic Party prepares for its 2028 presidential primary, recent polling errors in marquee midterm primary races have left Democrats wondering anew how polls will influence the field’s momentum.

The results in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial and Michigan’s Senate primaries were wildly off from what preelection polling had indicated. These misses raised the question of how much polls can be trusted, and it’s especially on the minds of Democratic campaign advisers and donors as the next presidential cycle approaches and they have to determine where to spend their time and money.

That might leave room for candidates to make the case that they’re competitive based on vibes and other metrics, like fundraising numbers, crowd sizes and number of online followers.

“We are going to enter an election season where there are a bajillion new sources of information, and no standard way to figure out which one means what,” said Ben Wikler, a former chair of the Wisconsin Democratic Party. “We're also going to be in a world where candidates and voters trusting their gut and making their case and seeing how the public responds will be more important than it ever was.”

Wikler watched as polls in his state didn’t capture what he thinks is the most telling measure of a candidate’s chances: conversations with voters.

“There was that kind of evidence on the ground that there was something happening and a new level of energy for Crowley in the final stretch that wasn't picked up in polls that closed a week before,” Wikler said.

Public polls in Wisconsin exaggerated Francesca Hong’s chances of beating David Crowley, the moderate candidate backed by the state’s governor, last week.

Hong, a democratic socialist who was projected to beat her primary opponents by double digits, narrowly lost to Crowley, who had only recently revived his campaign after suspending it.

In postmortem analyses, polling experts found that the Wisconsin polls — complicated by an evolving field of candidates — missed the undecided late voters who broke for Crowley. Wisconsin wasn’t an anomaly, either.

The other high-profile polling error occurred in another battleground state, Michigan, which will be one of the earliest states to vote in the Democratic nominating calendar in 2028.

Poll-defying performances have led to consequential victories for presidential candidates in battleground states like Wisconsin and Michigan. In 2016, polls consistently showed Hillary Clinton ahead of President Donald Trump in both states, which Trump ultimately won.

Since then, multiple cycles of mistaken polls may change how Democrats gauge momentum in what’s expected to be a crowded and unruly Democratic presidential primary field in 2028, particularly as polls have played such a key role in elevating candidates.

“Polls are a snapshot in time, and just kind of catch fire at the right moment, and all of a sudden they're polling in whatever high bracket, and then that helps them raise money, that helps them get on the debate stage, and it becomes this cycle,” a Democratic strategist who worked on past presidential campaigns said. “But that doesn't necessarily reward the best candidate.”

Polls can be consequential in a candidate’s strategy. Candidates use them to decide where to visit or spend money on advertisements, and in presidential elections, polls are one factor in deciding who qualifies to participate in a debate.

The best use of a poll is to show a campaign the voters they can still win over, said Charles Franklin, the director of the Marquette University Law School Poll.

“Sophisticated campaigns are using them to know which groups they still have the opportunity to influence,” Franklin said.

Trouble arises when campaigns treat polls as the only way to judge a campaign’s performance, some Democrats argue.

“The information you get from these public polls is one grain of sand in a beach of information about how to judge a candidate and a campaign, and too often it’s treated as the only piece of information that helps you tell the story of what’s going on,” said an adviser to a potential 2028 candidate who requested anonymity.

entries.title: Texas Families Ask the Supreme Court to Keep Ten Commandments Out of the Classroom
entries.summary: A lower court upheld a state law that requires public school classrooms to display a framed copy of the Ten Commandments.
entries.content:
More than two dozen Texas families on Monday asked the Supreme Court to review a state law requiring public school classrooms to display the Ten Commandments, in a case that could alter the separation between church and state.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas, along with several other legal and religious-liberty advocacy groups such as Americans United for Separation of Church and State, filed a petition that says a lower court ruling upholding the law “gutted the religious freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”

The filing contends the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals ignored a 1980 Supreme Court decision that struck down as unconstitutional a nearly identical Kentucky statute requiring the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.

The issues in the case would be of “exceptional national importance” for the high court to review, the plaintiffs said in the filing, since legislatures in dozens of states have considered laws on displaying the Ten Commandments over the past two years.

“If left in place, the decisions below could embolden state and local governments not only to enact more Ten Commandments laws, but to attempt other incursions on public-school families’ religious freedom, creating an administrative nightmare and litigation risk for school districts and diminishing, to an alarming extent, parents’ control over key aspects of their children’s religious education,” the filing says.

The 9-8 majority opinion in the 5th Circuit found that a 2022 Supreme Court decision allowing a high school football coach to engage in prayer with students made the precedent in the Kentucky case obsolete. The minority of the court held that only the Supreme Court, not a lower court, can overturn decisions from the nation’s highest court.

The families argue that in addition to “egregiously violat[ing]” Supreme Court precedent, the Texas state law infringes upon “both the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses of the First Amendment.”

The families attend 22 school districts across the state and come from Christian, Jewish, Hindu, Baha'i, Unitarian Universalist and nonreligious backgrounds. The petition groups together two separate but similar cases filed against the Texas state law.

“As a rabbi and parent, forcing a Christian version of the Ten Commandments on children in every classroom is particularly upsetting,” one of the plaintiffs, Rabbi Joshua Fixler, said.

The display of the Ten Commandments on government property has led to lengthy court battles across the nation. In 2001, then-Alabama Supreme Court Chief Justice Roy Moore installed a more than 5,000 pound monument of the Ten Commandments on the state’s judicial building grounds. Moore was removed from office in 2003 after refusing to comply with a federal court decision to remove the statue.

While the most recent copy of the Republican Party’s platform — released ahead of the 2024 election — does not explicitly advocate for the Ten Commandments to be displayed in classrooms, the document champions “the First Amendment Right to Pray and Read the Bible in school.”
